claim: Somatic mutations in the ESR1 (estrogen receptor alpha (ERα)) gene ligand-binding domain (LBD) represent a recognized mechanism of acquired resistance to endocrine therapy in breast cancer.
source: Somatic mutations in the ESR1 (estrogen receptor alpha (ERα)) gene ligand-binding domain (LBD) represent a recognized mechanism of acquired resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a recognized mechanism based on existing knowledge in the field.

claim: Bazedoxifene (BZA) possesses improved inhibitory potency against the Y537S and D538G ERα mutants compared to tamoxifen.
source: We found that BZA possesses improved inhibitory potency against the Y537S and D538G ERα mutants compared to tamoxifen and has additional inhibitory activity in combination with the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including reporter gene assays and cell proliferation studies.

claim: BZA has additional inhibitory activity in combination with the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib.
source: We found that BZA possesses improved inhibitory potency against the Y537S and D538G ERα mutants compared to tamoxifen and has additional inhibitory activity in combination with the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib.
evidence: This is supported by combination treatment experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: BZA's selective estrogen receptor degrading (SERD) properties override the stabilizing effects of the Y537S and D538G ERα mutations.
source: In addition, comprehensive biophysical and structural biology studies show BZA's selective estrogen receptor degrading (SERD) properties that override the stabilizing effects of the Y537S and D538G ERα mutations.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS, X-ray crystallography, and molecular dynamics simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: ERα plays critical roles in the etiology, treatment and prevention of the majority of breast cancers.
source: Estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) plays critical roles in the etiology, treatment and prevention of the majority of breast cancers (Frasor et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The majority of ER+ metastatic breast cancers that initially respond to endocrine treatment will become refractory despite continued ERα expression.
source: Unfortunately, the majority of ER+ metastatic breast cancers that initially respond to endocrine treatment will become refractory despite continued ERα expression (Toy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Somatic mutations to ESR1 ligand binding domain (LBD) were identified in 25–30% of patients who previously received endocrine treatment.
source: In addition, somatic mutations to ESR1 (gene for ERα) ligand binding domain (LBD) were identified in 25–30% of patients who previously received endocrine treatment (Toy et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2015; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Y537S and D538G are the two most prevalent ESR1 mutations.
source: Y537S and D538G are the two most prevalent mutations, and pre-clinical studies show that these mutations confer hormone-free transcriptional activity and relative resistance to tamoxifen and fulvestrant treatment (Toy et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2015; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Y537S and D538G mutations confer hormone-free transcriptional activity and relative resistance to tamoxifen and fulvestrant treatment.
source: Y537S and D538G are the two most prevalent mutations, and pre-clinical studies show that these mutations confer hormone-free transcriptional activity and relative resistance to tamoxifen and fulvestrant treatment (Toy et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2015; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pre-clinical studies.

claim: Both Y537S and D538G mutants enable constitutive ERα activity by favoring the agonist-like conformation of the receptor activating function-2 (AF-2) surface.
source: Both mutants enable constitutive ERα activity by favoring the agonist-like conformation of the receptor activating function-2 (AF-2) surface and significantly reduce hormone and 4-hydroxytamoxifen (the active metabolite of tamoxifen) binding affinities (Nettles et al., 2008; Fanning et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Y537S and D538G mutations significantly reduce hormone and 4-hydroxytamoxifen binding affinities.
source: Both mutants enable constitutive ERα activity by favoring the agonist-like conformation of the receptor activating function-2 (AF-2) surface and significantly reduce hormone and 4-hydroxytamoxifen (the active metabolite of tamoxifen) binding affinities (Nettles et al., 2008; Fanning et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous binding studies.

claim: Fulvestrant at high concentrations was the only molecule that reduced the Y537S and D538G ERα mutant transcriptional activity to basal levels in pre-clinical studies.
source: In pre-clinical studies, fulvestrant (FULV, a selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) and complete antiestrogen) at high concentrations was the only molecule that reduced the Y537S and D538G ERα mutant transcriptional activity to basal levels (Toy et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2015; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pre-clinical studies.

claim: Fulvestrant's clinical efficacy is limited by poor solubility and oral bioavailability.
source: However, its clinical efficacy is limited by poor solubility and oral bioavailability (Wardell et al., 2013a; van Kruchten et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pharmacological studies.

claim: BZA was approved for use in combination with conjugated equine estrogens for hormone replacement therapy in postmenopausal women in the US.
source: BZA was approved a number of years ago for the use in combination with conjugated equine estrogens for hormone replacement therapy in postmenopausal women (DUAVEE, Pfizer) in the US and for the prevention of osteoporosis as a single agent in Europe (Wardell et al., 2013a; Tikoo and Gupta, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to regulatory and clinical information.

claim: BZA was approved for the prevention of osteoporosis as a single agent in Europe.
source: BZA was approved a number of years ago for the use in combination with conjugated equine estrogens for hormone replacement therapy in postmenopausal women (DUAVEE, Pfizer) in the US and for the prevention of osteoporosis as a single agent in Europe (Wardell et al., 2013a; Tikoo and Gupta, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to regulatory and clinical information.

claim: BZA displayed strong antagonist and SERD profiles in the breast while retaining beneficial agonist properties in the bone.
source: Importantly, it displayed strong antagonist and SERD profiles in the breast while retaining beneficial agonist properties in the bone and did not stimulate endometrial tissue in pre-clinical studies (Wardell et al., 2013a; Komm et al., 2005; Lewis-Wambi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pre-clinical studies.

claim: BZA did not stimulate endometrial tissue in pre-clinical studies.
source: Importantly, it displayed strong antagonist and SERD profiles in the breast while retaining beneficial agonist properties in the bone and did not stimulate endometrial tissue in pre-clinical studies (Wardell et al., 2013a; Komm et al., 2005; Lewis-Wambi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pre-clinical studies.

claim: BZA showed potent antitumor activity in AI/SERM-resistant breast tumors in vivo.
source: In addition, BZA showed potent antitumor activity in AI/SERM-resistant breast tumors in vivo (Wardell et al., 2013b; Wardell et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo studies.

claim: BZA showed good oral bioavailability and improved pharmacokinetics compared with fulvestrant.
source: Further, BZA showed good oral bioavailability and improved pharmacokinetics compared with fulvestrant (FULV) (Wardell et al., 2013a; Biskobing, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pharmacological studies.

claim: BZA was a more potent inhibitor of WT ERα transcription than either 4-OHT or FULV in MCF7 cells expressing an ERE-luciferase reporter gene.
source: In MCF7 cells that expressed an ERE-luciferase reporter gene, BZA was a more potent inhibitor of WT ERα transcription than either 4-OHT or FULV (inhibition of luciferase IC50 for BZA = 0.12 nM, 4-OHT = 0.39 nM and FULV = 0.76 nM) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inhibition of luciferase IC50 for BZA is 0.12 nM in MCF7 cells expressing an ERE-luciferase reporter gene.
source: In MCF7 cells that expressed an ERE-luciferase reporter gene, BZA was a more potent inhibitor of WT ERα transcription than either 4-OHT or FULV (inhibition of luciferase IC50 for BZA = 0.12 nM, 4-OHT = 0.39 nM and FULV = 0.76 nM) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inhibition of luciferase IC50 for 4-OHT is 0.39 nM in MCF7 cells expressing an ERE-luciferase reporter gene.
source: In MCF7 cells that expressed an ERE-luciferase reporter gene, BZA was a more potent inhibitor of WT ERα transcription than either 4-OHT or FULV (inhibition of luciferase IC50 for BZA = 0.12 nM, 4-OHT = 0.39 nM and FULV = 0.76 nM) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inhibition of luciferase IC50 for FULV is 0.76 nM in MCF7 cells expressing an ERE-luciferase reporter gene.
source: In MCF7 cells that expressed an ERE-luciferase reporter gene, BZA was a more potent inhibitor of WT ERα transcription than either 4-OHT or FULV (inhibition of luciferase IC50 for BZA = 0.12 nM, 4-OHT = 0.39 nM and FULV = 0.76 nM) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: For cyclin D1, 4-OHT increased the mRNA level at 10−8 M and showed little effect at 10−6M in MCF-7 cells.
source: For cyclin D1, 4-OHT increased the mRNA level at 10−8 M and showed little effect at 10−6M, while both FULV and BZA decreased mRNA levels at 10−6 M (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both FULV and BZA decreased cyclin D1 mRNA levels at 10−6 M in MCF-7 cells.
source: For cyclin D1, 4-OHT increased the mRNA level at 10−8 M and showed little effect at 10−6M, while both FULV and BZA decreased mRNA levels at 10−6 M (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BZA increased c-myc mRNA levels at 10−8 M while it significantly decreased c-myc mRNA at 10−6 M in MCF-7 cells.
source: BZA increased c-myc mRNA levels at 10−8 M while it significantly decreased c-myc mRNA at 10−6 M (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 10−6 M BZA showed the greatest reduction in mRNA levels of both CA12 and GREB compared to 4-OHT and FULV in MCF-7 cells.
source: Interestingly, 10−6 M BZA showed the greatest reduction in mRNA levels of both CA12 and GREB compared to 4-OHT and FULV (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: BZA mediated similar levels of ERα degradation compared to FULV in MCF7 cells.
source: Overall, BZA mediated similar levels of ERα degradation compared to FULV (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: BZA showed an improved IC50 for cell growth inhibition compared to 4-OHT and in the same range as fulvestrant in MCF7 cells.
source: In terms of cell growth inhibition, BZA showed an improved IC50 compared to 4-OHT and in the same range as fulvestrant (BZA IC50 = 2.4×10−10 M, FULV IC50 = 3.1×10−10 M and 4-OHT IC50 = 1.19×10−9 M (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: BZA IC50 for cell growth inhibition is 2.4×10−10 M in MCF7 cells.
source: In terms of cell growth inhibition, BZA showed an improved IC50 compared to 4-OHT and in the same range as fulvestrant (BZA IC50 = 2.4×10−10 M, FULV IC50 = 3.1×10−10 M and 4-OHT IC50 = 1.19×10−9 M (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 1G.

claim: FULV IC50 for cell growth inhibition is 3.1×10−10 M in MCF7 cells.
source: In terms of cell growth inhibition, BZA showed an improved IC50 compared to 4-OHT and in the same range as fulvestrant (BZA IC50 = 2.4×10−10 M, FULV IC50 = 3.1×10−10 M and 4-OHT IC50 = 1.19×10−9 M (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 4-OHT IC50 for cell growth inhibition is 1.19×10−9 M in MCF7 cells.
source: In terms of cell growth inhibition, BZA showed an improved IC50 compared to 4-OHT and in the same range as fulvestrant (BZA IC50 = 2.4×10−10 M, FULV IC50 = 3.1×10−10 M and 4-OHT IC50 = 1.19×10−9 M (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 1G.

claim: BZA demonstrated an increased potency for inhibiting Y537S mutant cell growth compared to FULV and 4-OHT, with an IC50 of 1 × 10−10 M vs 2 × 10−9 M and 7 × 10−9 M, respectively.
source: BZA demonstrated an increased potency compared to FULV and 4-OHT, with an IC50 of 1 × 10−10 M vs 2 × 10−9 M and 7 × 10−9 M, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data in MCF7 cells expressing Y537S mutant shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BZA inhibited the transcription of ERα target genes cyclin D1, c-Myc, and PR in cells expressing the Y537S mutant in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In addition, qPCR data showed that BZA inhibited the transcription of ERα target genes cyclin D1, c-Myc, and PR, in cells expressing the Y537S mutant, in a dose-dependent manner, confirming the on-target effects of BZA in the presence of the mutation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In cells expressing HA-WT ERα, BZA and FULV induced degradation of the receptor to similar levels.
source: In cells expressing HA-WT ERα, BZA and FULV induced degradation of the receptor to similar levels while the amount of the receptor increased upon 4-OHT treatment and was slightly reduced with E2 and RAL (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The amount of WT ERα receptor increased upon 4-OHT treatment in MCF-7 cells.
source: In cells expressing HA-WT ERα, BZA and FULV induced degradation of the receptor to similar levels while the amount of the receptor increased upon 4-OHT treatment and was slightly reduced with E2 and RAL (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: For the Y537S mutant, ERα expression remained unchanged for E2 and FULV treatment.
source: Interestingly, for the Y537S mutant, ERα expression remained unchanged for E2 and FULV, while it increased for 4-OHT and RAL.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Y537S ERα expression increased with 4-OHT and RAL treatment.
source: Interestingly, for the Y537S mutant, ERα expression remained unchanged for E2 and FULV, while it increased for 4-OHT and RAL.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Y537S ERα increased with BZA but less so than RAL or 4-OHT.
source: Y537S ERα also increased with BZA but less so than RAL or 4-OHT.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: BZA degraded the D538G ERα mutant to a greater extent than FULV.
source: Surprisingly, BZA degraded the D538G ERα mutant to a greater extent than FULV, while 4-OHT and RAL both increased its expression after 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: 4-OHT and RAL both increased D538G ERα expression after 24 hr.
source: Surprisingly, BZA degraded the D538G ERα mutant to a greater extent than FULV, while 4-OHT and RAL both increased its expression after 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Near complete ERα degradation was observed at 25 nM BZA in T47D, ZR75-1, CAMA-1, and MDA-MB-361 cells.
source: In each cell line, near complete degradation was observed at 25 nM BZA.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The combination of BZA and PB demonstrated the greatest arrest in cellular proliferation in MCF-7, ZR75, and T47D cell lines.
source: For the first three cell lines, the combination of BZA and PB demonstrated the greatest arrest in cellular proliferation, whereas for the LTED cells it was comparable to PB+ FULV (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figures 3A-D.

claim: For LTED cells, the combination of BZA and PB was comparable to PB+ FULV in arresting cellular proliferation.
source: For the first three cell lines, the combination of BZA and PB demonstrated the greatest arrest in cellular proliferation, whereas for the LTED cells it was comparable to PB+ FULV (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figures 3A-D.

claim: Reduced proliferation of MCF-7 cells expressing the Y537S mutant was observed for the BZA +PB treatment compared to all other treatments.
source: Additionally, reduced proliferation of MCF-7 cells expressing the Y537S mutant was observed for the BZA +PB treatment compared to all other treatments (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: BZA had superior activity in the inhibition of ER transcriptional activity compared to fulvestrant in MCF7 cells.
source: Transcriptional reporter gene assays in MCF7 cells showed that: 1. BZA had superior activity in the inhibition of ER transcriptional activity compared to fulvestrant.
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene assay data shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: Palbociclib does not affect ER transcriptional activity either as a single agent or in combination with BZA.
source: In addition, palbociclib does not affect ER transcriptional activity either as a single agent or in combination with BZA (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene assay data shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: Treatment with PB does not affect BZA or FULV-induced degradation of ERα.
source: Similarly, immunoblotting for ER showed that treatment with PB does not affect BZA or FULV-induced degradation of ERα (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Dose-dependent inhibition of co-regulator binding was observed for the majority of co-regulator peptides with 4-OHT, BZA and FULV.
source: Overall, dose-dependent inhibition of co-regulator binding was observed for the majority of co-regulator peptides with the three drugs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by MARCoNI assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EC50 levels for FULV in both the WT and mutant cells was higher compared to SERMs.
source: A comparison of EC50 levels for inhibition of co-regulator binding of the three ER antagonists showed that EC50 levels for FULV in both the WT and mutant cells was higher, as expected given the mechanism of action of FULV, compared to SERMs.
evidence: This is supported by MARCoNI assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 4-OHT and BZA EC50s were higher in the presence of the Y537S and D538G mutations.
source: The 4-OHT and BZA EC50s were higher in the presence of the Y537S and D538G mutations.
evidence: This is supported by MARCoNI assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the absence of hormone, SRC3 did not bind to WT ERα LBD.
source: Previously, we showed that in the absence of hormone, SRC3 did not bind to WT ERα LBD, whereas Y537S ERα bound SRC3 markedly in the absence of E2 with a 10-fold reduced affinity, and D538G ERα bound SRC3 with a 100-fold reduced affinity compared to hormone-bound WT receptor (Fanning et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous FRET assay data.

claim: Y537S ERα bound SRC3 markedly in the absence of E2 with a 10-fold reduced affinity compared to hormone-bound WT receptor.
source: Previously, we showed that in the absence of hormone, SRC3 did not bind to WT ERα LBD, whereas Y537S ERα bound SRC3 markedly in the absence of E2 with a 10-fold reduced affinity, and D538G ERα bound SRC3 with a 100-fold reduced affinity compared to hormone-bound WT receptor (Fanning et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous FRET assay data.

claim: D538G ERα bound SRC3 with a 100-fold reduced affinity compared to hormone-bound WT receptor.
source: Previously, we showed that in the absence of hormone, SRC3 did not bind to WT ERα LBD, whereas Y537S ERα bound SRC3 markedly in the absence of E2 with a 10-fold reduced affinity, and D538G ERα bound SRC3 with a 100-fold reduced affinity compared to hormone-bound WT receptor (Fanning et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous FRET assay data.

claim: 4-OHT, BZA and RAL reversed the binding of SRC3 NRD to the two mutant ERs and WT-ERα with similar potencies.
source: 4-OHT, BZA and RAL reversed the binding of SRC3 NRD to the two mutant ERs and WT-ERα with similar potencies (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The affinities of RAL, BZA and FULV for the ERα mutants were reduced 9 to 27-fold relative to WT-ERα.
source: The affinities of RAL, BZA and FULV for the ERα mutants were reduced 9 to 27-fold relative to WT-ERα.
evidence: This is supported by competitive ligand binding assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: The binding affinity of 4-OHT remained the highest compared to RAL, BZA and FULV against the mutant LBDs.
source: It should be noted that the binding affinity of 4-OHT remained the highest compared to RAL, BZA and FULV against the mutant LBDs.
evidence: This is supported by competitive ligand binding assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: The binding affinities of all tested antiestrogens were somewhat more reduced in D538G than in Y537S.
source: The binding affinities of all tested antiestrogens were somewhat more reduced in D538G than in Y537S.
evidence: This is supported by competitive ligand binding assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: An X-ray crystal structure for the WT ERα LBD in complex with BZA was solved to 2.4 Å with two dimers in the asymmetric unit.
source: An X-ray crystal structure for the WT ERα LBD, in complex with BZA was solved to 2.4 Å with two dimers in the asymmetric unit (ASU) (PDB: 4XI3).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray crystallography data deposited as PDB: 4XI3.

claim: The distal phenol on BZA appears to form a hydrogen bond with improved binding geometry to H524 compared to the distal phenol of RAL.
source: Interestingly, the distal phenol on BZA appears to form a hydrogen bond with improved binding geometry to H524 compared to the distal phenol of RAL.
evidence: This is inferred from the X-ray crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 5.

claim: The azepan ring of BZA pushes against V534 and P535.
source: The core differences for BZA broadcast down the linker arm to alter its vector towards H12 where the azepan ring now pushes against V534 and P535 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray crystal structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The alterations to V534 and P535 propagate to H12 which appears displaced out of the AF-2 cleft into a less stable orientation.
source: The alterations to V534 and P535 propagate to H12 which appears displaced out of the AF-2 cleft into a less stable orientation.
evidence: This is inferred from the X-ray crystal structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: A significant energetic shift was observed between the dihedral scans of BZA and RAL, revealing that the BZA arm can adopt a set of torsion angles with significantly reduced energetic penalties compared to RAL.
source: A significant energetic shift was observed between the dihedral scans, revealing that the BZA arm can adopt a set of torsion angles with significantly reduced energetic penalties compared to RAL (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by quantum mechanical calculations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The energetic minima well is significantly broader for BZA compared to RAL.
source: Importantly, the energetic minima well is significantly broader for BZA compared to RAL, indicating that the angles adopted by BZA in the ERα ligand-binding site are more favorable than RAL.
evidence: This is supported by quantum mechanical calculations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: An energetic penalty of approximately 1 kcal/mol would be incurred by RAL to adopt the same conformation observed for BZA in the X-ray crystal structure.
source: Furthermore, an energetic penalty of approximately 1 kcal/mol would be incurred by RAL to adopt the same conformation observed for BZA in the X-ray crystal structure.
evidence: This is supported by quantum mechanical calculations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Addition of E2 resulted in an increased protection against exchange in H12 of ERα, and this protection was enhanced for the Y537S and D538G mutants.
source: As expected, addition of E2 resulted in an increased protection against exchange in H12 (inferred as increased stability or less dynamic), and this protection was enhanced for the Y537S and D538G mutants (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6.

claim: FULV treatment led to increased D2O uptake in H12 of regions near H12 in both the WT and D538G mutant.
source: Also, FULV treatment led to increased D2O uptake in H12 (interpreted as destabilization) of regions near H12 in both the WT and D538G mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with its SERD-like properties.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding of 4-OHT resulted in decreased stability of H12 with the Y537S compared to D538G and WT receptor.
source: Similar to previously published data (Fanning et al., 2016), binding of 4-OHT resulted in decreased stability of H12 with the Y537S compared to D538G and WT receptor (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these mutants resist the ability of the SERM to alter their structure.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and a citation to previous work.

claim: Addition of BZA did not increase the stability of the region near H12 to as great of an extent as 4-OHT in WT and mutant ERα LBDs.
source: Interestingly, addition of BZA did not increase the stability (lesser protection) of the region near H12 to as great of an extent as 4-OHT in WT and mutant ERα LBDs, suggesting that BZA-bound ERα adopts a less stable antagonist conformation than 4-OHT-bound ERα (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), consistent with the crystal structure.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: BZA-bound ERα adopts a less stable antagonist conformation than 4-OHT-bound ERα.
source: Interestingly, addition of BZA did not increase the stability (lesser protection) of the region near H12 to as great of an extent as 4-OHT in WT and mutant ERα LBDs, suggesting that BZA-bound ERα adopts a less stable antagonist conformation than 4-OHT-bound ERα (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), consistent with the crystal structure.
evidence: This is inferred from HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: H12 of both BZA-bound Y537S and D538G mutants remain close to an antagonist conformation according to MD simulations.
source: MD simulations show that H12 of both BZA-bound mutants remain close to an antagonist conformation (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figures 7B and 7D.

claim: H12 conformational fluctuations observed in MD simulations are less pronounced in Y537S-BZA than they are in D538G-BZA.
source: Furthermore, H12 conformational fluctuations observed in MD simulations are less pronounced in Y537S-BZA than they are in D538G-BZA (Figure 7C), which echoes the aforementioned reduced H12 dynamics observed in HDX-MS data and agrees with our result that Y537S reduces BZA activity more than D538G does.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Over the course of the simulations, the Y537S-BZA structure shows a hydrogen bond formation between E380 and S537.
source: Over the course of the simulations, the Y537S-BZA structure shows a hydrogen bond formation between E380 and S537 (Figure 7B), which could contribute to fewer H12 conformational fluctuations in Y537S ERα.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The predicted hydrogen bond between E380 and S537 may stabilize H12 in the AF-2 cleft relative to WT.
source: This predicted hydrogen bond may stabilize H12 in the AF-2 cleft relative to WT.
evidence: This is inferred from molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The D538G mutation increases the conformational variance of the H11-12 loop compared to Y537S.
source: The D538G mutation further increases the conformational variance of the H11-12 loop compared to Y537S (Figure 7C), which can be explained by the lack of a hydrogen bond in Y537S and the greater backbone conformational freedom allowed by the mutant glycine residue.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The H11-12 loop of both Y537S and D538G appears further away from the protein core and BZA compared to that of WT.
source: Additionally, the H11-12 loop of both Y537S and D538G appears further away from the protein core and BZA compared to that of WT (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figures 7B and 7D.

claim: Both Y537S and D538G mutations produce a stable antagonist conformation, especially at H12.
source: Together, these data show that both mutations produce a stable antagonist conformation, especially at H12, and reduce the SERD-like properties of BZA by lessening its ability to disrupt the H11-12 loop and stabilize H12 in the AF-2 cleft.
evidence: This is inferred from molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Y537S and D538G mutations reduce the SERD-like properties of BZA by lessening its ability to disrupt the H11-12 loop and stabilize H12 in the AF-2 cleft.
source: Together, these data show that both mutations produce a stable antagonist conformation, especially at H12, and reduce the SERD-like properties of BZA by lessening its ability to disrupt the H11-12 loop and stabilize H12 in the AF-2 cleft.
evidence: This is inferred from molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Newly characterized orally available pure antiestrogens (e.g. GDC-0927, AZ9496, and RAD1901) are emerging as potentially potent inhibitors of Y537S and D538G mutants.
source: Newly characterized orally available pure antiestrogens (e.g. GDC-0927, AZ9496, and RAD1901) are emerging as potentially potent inhibitors of these mutants, but their long-term clinical utility is unknown and their side effect profiles have not been studied in large patient populations (Toy et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BZA is already clinically approved for use in hormone replacement therapy.
